text:
You don't have to sit on 0% while you wait for an entry.

There are 3 places paying around 8% on stablecoins right now, with no leverage.

The best one isn't the highest rate.

1. USD1 on Dolomite (Ethereum), ~8% APR

The simplest one. Deposit $USD1 into @Dolomite_io's lending market and earn interest from borrowers.

The 8% is about 3.8% lending interest plus 4.3% in rewards.

~$319M supplied and ~$51M sitting available, so getting out shouldn't be a problem.

The catch is over half the yield is rewards, claimed separately through Merkl. Without them you're closer to 3.8%.

2. Plume x Re7 vault on Kamino (Solana), ~8.2% APY

Deposit $USDC into the Plume x Re7 USDC vault in @kamino's Earn section. About 3.8% is borrower interest and 4.4% is incentives. ~$7.8M in it.

Heads up, the 90-day average is 6%. Treat 8.2% as lasting about as long as the incentives do.

3. ONyc on Loopscale (Solana), ~8.3% APY

@onrefinance's $ONyc earns yield from reinsurance, basically the premiums insurance companies pay to protect themselves.

On @Loopscale you deposit $USDC, borrowers put up ONyc as collateral, and the interest they pay is your yield. Almost all of it is real lending interest, not rewards.

The catch is it's 98% lent out, so only ~$390K of $24M can come out right now. Size it small.

If you want more and can wait, @Rockaway_X's OnRe Core Vault has averaged ~11% over the past month, with a 7-day wait to redeem.

Which would you use?

If you're parking cash for a better entry, getting it back fast matters more than squeezing out another 2-3%. That's Dolomite or Kamino.

None of this is risk-free. Smart contract bugs, depegs, falling yields, and thin withdrawal liquidity can all bite.

Where are you parking your stables right now?

text:
Anthropic 平台工程负责人 Katelyn Lesse：上千个 AI 智能体一起干活，还缺程序员解决四个难题

AI 越来越会写代码，很多程序员开始怀疑自己的手艺还值不值钱。Anthropic 平台工程负责人 Katelyn Lesse 10 月 25 日发文说，她看到的情况正相反：接下来一两年，AI 想做成大事，得先靠程序员解决一批新问题。她说，现在是当工程师最有意思的时候之一。

Lesse 在 Anthropic 负责平台工程，据她接受 Kleiner Perkins 访谈时的介绍，团队约 200 人。她此前在 Stripe 和 Betterment 带过工程团队。这篇文章发在她的个人博客和 X 上，X 上阅读量约 61 万。

【这些问题从哪来】

AI 智能体，就是能自己调用工具、一步步完成任务的 AI 程序。Lesse 说，它最早只是聊天框，人盯着一问一答；后来模型能独立干更久、更难的活，开始搬到云端运行；再往后出现了多智能体系统：一个总管 AI 把任务拆开，分给一批助手去做，还有的 AI 专门负责打分、提建议。

她说，现在已经有人在搭由成千上万个智能体组成、连续工作不停的系统，用来做科研、新发现和硬件设计。规模一上来，就冒出了四类新问题。

【难题一：服务器怎么安排】

现在大部分软件跑在 Kubernetes 上，这是一套给服务器排班的系统，擅长管“一模一样的副本，哪个挂了换一个顶上”。Lesse 说智能体正好相反：每个都是独一份，记着自己干到哪了；大量时间在等模型回话、等工具、等别的智能体或等人回复，闲多久说不准，忙起来又可能一下冒出几千个。

Google 上个月开源的 Agent Substrate 就是冲这个问题做的。据 Google 官方博客，它能让闲着的智能体休眠、把资源腾出来，需要时半秒内唤醒。Lesse 说这块还有大量问题没解决。

【难题二：谁在干活，能干什么】

很多智能体用的是人的账号和权限，系统得分清某个操作是人做的，还是 AI 替人做的。更难的是授权：一个系统替你连干几周，你怎么事先讲清它能做什么、不能做什么？智能体之间互相派活时，一个智能体凭什么相信另一个？Lesse 说，确认身份可以借用现成技术，比如用很快过期的临时凭证代替长期有效的密钥；授权这块基本还是空白。

【难题三：一个被骗，全队遭殃】

Lesse 说，最近几个月，尤其最近几周，软件漏洞冒出来的速度超过了业界修补的速度，很多出在大量系统依赖的核心软件里。本月 PHP、GitLab、Node.js 就接连发布了严重漏洞的修复。上千个智能体跑在这些软件上，还要写来路不明的代码、读来路不明的网页，没修好的漏洞就危险得多。

多智能体还多一层风险：一个智能体被网页里藏的恶意指令骗了，可能把指令转给同伴，甚至写进共享记忆，让后来的智能体也照做。她的建议是让每个智能体在严格隔离的“沙箱”里干活，好比实验室把每份样本放进独立的密封箱，一个出事不会传染整屋。

【难题四：跑偏了要能叫停】

系统得记下每个智能体做了什么，而且任何智能体都改不了自己或别人的记录。还得有一个总闸，监控一发现问题，就能把整个系统一次停下，收回所有权限。Lesse 说最难的是判断系统有没有跑偏：一个智能体反复尝试访问不在白名单里的网站，可能是在搞破坏，也可能只是太想把任务做完。

文章最后，Lesse 对正在焦虑的工程师说，这些领域大多还没有现成答案，值得钻进去学、形成自己的判断。

Agent Substrate 官方介绍：https://t.co/M5LtIg57lH

text:
This person is challenged, so let’s help him understand, so others avoid the same pitfall

As we do that, you’ll see how this graph is much worse than it looks at first sight in 2 ways

When we talk about crime and immigration, the underlying question is:
Who should we let in?

A person that commits 20x more crime than the average native is very bad. Don’t get these people in. 

Now, if you only have 10 of them, are they yet a national threat? No, they’re not.

Can they become one?
Surely, if you only let in people like them. 
So by talking about the per capita, you’re raising the alarm. 

Another way to say the same thing: if a woman finds herself alone at night in the subway, and she can choose between one wagon with a native and one with an afghan asylum seeker, which one should she choose? By far, she will be safer with the native. 

Does it mean the majority of rapes are committed by Afghans? No! There are too few. Thankfully! If there were as many as natives, the rape rate would be 10-20x higher. 

So yes, you’re more likely to be raped by a native because there are many more. 

Now the types of rapes. Broadly there are 2: from ppl you know, and from ppl you don’t know. 

I’d argue the rapes from ppl you don’t know are much scarier, because you have zero agency on them, because there are few choices you can make differently to avoid them, short of curtailing your daily life. 

Meanwhile, you have some agency with partners: don’t start relationships with bad people, leave them, don’t contact them, call for help…

I assume the natives tend to commit more of this type of crime, whereas immigrants commit more rapes to strangers. Therefore not only are these immigrants more likely to commit rape, they’re also more likely to commit the worst type of rape—to strangers.

And when we have public debates on these things, public behavior is much more relevant than private behavior, so this type of rape is much more relevant to public debate than the more private one (even if both are relevant). 

So yes, this graph is bad because it’s logarithmic and undersells the problem, but also because this blends both stranger and acquainted rape. If you only look at stranger rape, immigrants would likely be even worse. 

And yet, also, as a woman you’re more likely to be raped by somebody who knows you, so beware

KALSHI ANNOUNCED PARTNERSHIP WITH S&P DOW JONES INDICES

The partnership will introduce indices built from prediction market contracts, covering politics, AI, and economic events 

This will pave the way for ETFs and other financial products tied to real-world events. https://t.co/HB5rVozknM
author: DeFiMidas
quoted_text:
S&P Dow Jones Indices and Kalshi are joining forces to build the next generation of financial markets.

The Dow launched in 1896. The S&P 500 in 1957. The idea was simple: bring individual stocks together into a single benchmark, giving people a clearer view of the broader market.

Over time, products built around those benchmarks transformed investing. Index funds, ETFs, futures, and options gave investors ways to gain diversified market exposure and hedge broad market swings.

These indices became foundations of global finance. More than $20 trillion is indexed or benchmarked to the S&P 500 alone.

Today, this structure extends beyond stocks to bonds, commodities, currencies, and more.

The next step is to bring that structure to the events that shape everyone’s lives.

Through this partnership, S&P Dow Jones Indices and Kalshi will work together to create indices composed of Kalshi event contracts.

Think about what that opens up.

An index of political power. An index of supply chain risk. An index tracking AI’s impact on employment. An index of sports outcomes that affect broadcasters, advertisers, cities, and small businesses. An index of weather risks that shape harvests, energy demand, and business revenues.

Each would bundle event contracts into a single indicator, helping people understand how related risks are evolving.

Over time, products built around these indices could offer diversified exposure to those events and new ways to hedge their impact.

The events that shape our lives could become as easy to track and gain exposure to as the S&P 500.

text:
S&P Dow Jones Indices and Kalshi are joining forces to build the next generation of financial markets.

The Dow launched in 1896. The S&P 500 in 1957. The idea was simple: bring individual stocks together into a single benchmark, giving people a clearer view of the broader market.

Over time, products built around those benchmarks transformed investing. Index funds, ETFs, futures, and options gave investors ways to gain diversified market exposure and hedge broad market swings.

These indices became foundations of global finance. More than $20 trillion is indexed or benchmarked to the S&P 500 alone.

Today, this structure extends beyond stocks to bonds, commodities, currencies, and more.

The next step is to bring that structure to the events that shape everyone’s lives.

Through this partnership, S&P Dow Jones Indices and Kalshi will work together to create indices composed of Kalshi event contracts.

Think about what that opens up.

An index of political power. An index of supply chain risk. An index tracking AI’s impact on employment. An index of sports outcomes that affect broadcasters, advertisers, cities, and small businesses. An index of weather risks that shape harvests, energy demand, and business revenues.

Each would bundle event contracts into a single indicator, helping people understand how related risks are evolving.

Over time, products built around these indices could offer diversified exposure to those events and new ways to hedge their impact.

The events that shape our lives could become as easy to track and gain exposure to as the S&P 500.

text:
Idk who needs to hear this, but formal verification of software (mathematically checking that software is correct) is by no means done, even now that we have LLMs and the proof tedium is gone. Instead, having LLMs lets us focus on the spec, where humans remain in the loop, and where people were often sloppy in the past. By sloppy I mean they often touted “formally verified!!11”, without even mentioning the spec. And upon closer inspection, the spec often turned out to miss critical guarantees you would naturally expect.

Formal verification IS hard. First, you need to figure out what behavior you even want to check: the spec. Then, you need to go through the tedium of writing a proof that your program indeed satisfies the spec.

LLMs massively speed up the second step. That’s because the proof can automatically be checked by a compiler. If the compiler is happy, the LLM did its job and you can trust the result, namely that your program satisfies the spec, without reading the proof yourself. (Ofc assuming you don't hit a compiler bug.)

But the first step is still there: What’s the spec? Writing the spec is still tedious and error-prone, and while LLMs help, a human needs to remain in the loop, at least to some extent, to assess whether the spec matches with the programmer's intention and the user's expectation. If you vibe that part, that’s where the bugs will creep back in.

Also: not all specs are equal. Don't trust "formally verified" without checking the spec. If the spec only says "the program doesn't crash", that is much less useful than a spec that reflects in detail the intended and expected functionality of the program.

So, humans are not leaving the loop, we're just moving up a level. With the proof tedium gone, we can finally focus our attention on the spec!

author: TheDavidTai
quoted_text:
Big win for local LLM inference!

This new inference engine runs LLMs 4x faster than llama.cpp:

I ran Qwen3.5 9B on a base M5 MacBook Pro with three engines:

- llama.cpp: 22.0 tokens/s
- MLX: 25.1 tokens/s
- uzu: 92.1 tokens/s

The video below shows all three runs side by side.

The first two numbers don't mean llama.cpp or MLX are badly built. But both are sitting right under a hard limit of local decoding.

When an LLM generates text, every new token needs one full pass through the model, and that pass reads all of the model's weights from memory.

A base M5 reads memory at about 153 GB/s. A 4-bit 9B model weighs about 5.2 GB.

So at one token per pass, the ceiling is roughly 153 ÷ 5.2 ≈ 29 tokens/s, however fast the GPU computes.

uzu gets past that ceiling by producing several tokens per pass instead of one:

↳ A small drafter (DFlash) proposes candidates for the next 16 positions at once.

↳ A tiny adapter (Weaver, 56.7M params) picks among them left to right, so the guesses form coherent text, and keeps a few alternative branches as a tree.

↳ The 9B model checks the whole tree in a single pass and keeps the longest path it agrees with. The main model still decides every token that ends up in the output.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/TKikR80qEA

(don't forget to star it 🌟)

In my run, each pass of the 9B model produced 7.5 tokens on average. Ordinary decoding produces exactly 1.

The weights and kernels are designed around this too. uzu ships its own 4-bit checkpoints, and on M5 chips it runs the verification step on the GPU's int8 matrix path.

uzu is an open-source inference engine by Mirai Labs, written in Rust with Metal kernels. It has Swift, Python, TypeScript and Rust bindings, so the same engine runs inside a Mac or iOS app.

I shared the GitHub repo above.

If you want to dive deeper, my co-founder wrote a detailed breakdown of why local inference is memory-bound and how uzu's speculative decoding gets past it.

Read it below.

text:
Your window to prepare, even with the basics, is closing.

For those tracking the indicators that an event is increasingly likely, you know that it is now undeniable that something is brewing. It has now reached the point to where national governments are now overtly telling civilians to make preparations, however basic. 

As part of my career in the US intelligence community, one of things I supported was Counterintelligence threats to Continuity of Government (COG) and Continuity of Operations (COOP). Something i can say for absolute certain is that once governments signal that their citizens need to prepare, those preparations have already been conducted for national leadership.

Governments plan for two course of action; bug in and bug out. Bug in involves hunkering down where they are. They lock down the facility. No one in and no one out. Bug out involves the relocation to a secure location that is away from potential threats, which includes hungry people. They lock down. No one in. No one out. 

It would be wise for you to assess your current situation and decide the appropriate course of action for yourself and family. 

What has been happening over the past several years is that the affluent have been making their own preparations for crisis, including efforts to secure survivable locations away from major population centers, storing food, water, and the means to defend those locations. 

The most recent loud signals are likely our last real warning. Governments from Eastern Europe to the UK are now telling people to have the basics on hand to weather a bad situation. Notably, this is on the back drop, for those that remember, when "prepping" was aligned with anti-government extremism under the Obama administration. What you will notice over the next several weeks is the expanding time period that governments call for people to prepare. In Europe, its currently between 3 days and a week. However, the US just sent the loudest signal concerning how significant the situation is; military bases must be self-sufficient for 90 days. The gravity of this can't be understated. 

The calls for preparedness will escalate in their time frames. 3 days will turn into a week. A week will turn in to a few weeks. A few weeks into a couple months.

What Americans should know is that you will be on your own. FEMA does not have the resources to help people in a time of need during an event at national scale. You local authorities don't either. 

For those in major cities, you should know that almost two decades ago now the Asymmetric Warfare Group, in collaboration with the US military, conducted a study on the process that major population centers descend into chaos, anchored on the current "just in time" supply chain. In 3 days, a major city is out of food in the major stores. Looting starts, first whats left on shelves, then people start taking from one another. Suburbia is then the next harvest location. People organize and target food distribution warehouses. Then people head out into the country where people are prepared and things get ugly. 

My recommendation for people is to not focus on the "what", the catalyst for crisis. Focus on being prepared and prepare quietly. Those who fail to prepare will target those who they know are. This includes your own family members. You, at some point, will hear, "well if something happens, I'll just come to your house", stated as a joke. But this is not a joke. You have now become someone's backup plan. Don't allow this. 

Right now, you need to shift your mental paradigm. Randomize when you go to the store. Avoid dark hours. Slow down how many times Amazon deliveries show up at your house. And start to think about how to feign poverty. Affluence/comfort has a signature that is easy to spot and smell. 

You can't prepare forever. Even governments don't do that. What you need to do is prepare to weather the storm. As the saying in the military goes, "KISS"; Keep It Simple, Stupid. Water, rice, protein, canned foods. Then think basic medicines for colds, flu, and infections. Then think protection and communications. You don't need thousands of dollars, you just need to be smart.  

I've recommended this before, but I will say it again. Go watch two movies; "The Day After" and "Threads". This is not to scare you. This is so you can notice the indicators leading up to crisis. They are quiet at first. Governments say everything is fine. Then they say have basic preparations. Then they say have more because help wont be coming immediately. Most people will brush it off and just say it will pass. We are now at the part of both movies where governments are telling people to prepare and some degree of panic is setting in. This will get worse. 

You must identify your phase line for action. Assuming, in any way, that crisis will hit and the government will show up to rescue you is a mistake. Turn that fear you are feeling into focused action.

For those that are prepared, keep preparing and be quiet. For those that are unprepared, start now and be quiet. 

For everyone, hang in there. Its going to get rough. 🥃

text:
As I - along with all public analysts - continue to pore over the Anthropic $ANT S-1 - some thoughts / observations:

The principal question for Anthropic: ultimately boils down to will their revenues generated outpace their fixed compute commitments? This is the principal dilemma Dario lays out in his interview with Dwarkesh. Procure too little and you run the risk that you are under resourced in a race against other AI labs - and forced to procure compute at any price into an already tight market (aka Anthropic this year). Provision too much relative to your revenue traction and you run the risk of “blowing up”.

Compute Qualities

Compute for an AI Lab generally has the following characteristics:
• Take or pay contracts - given provider fulfills performance SLAs
• Annual cost of usually 1/4 of the capex required - on a rolling basis (owned / leased chip math)
• Configuration of counterparty (hyperscaler, neocloud, self-build) and accelerator (Nvidia GPU, Hyperscaler ASIC (TPU, Trainium), 3rd Party Accelerator (Cerebras, etc), AMD GPU)
• In general, self-build allows the labs (and the hyperscalers) the flexibility to “smooth” the existential curve. Building shell buys an AI lab / hyperscaler flexibility to adapt to their business needs. Contrary to fanatical consensus that there are “GPUs gathering dust and being hoarded” - the biggest cost in a DC is the depreciation of IT gear. Quite catastrophically money losing - vs over building land, power, shell but not equipping with IT gear (~20% of capex in land / power / shell depreciated over 10-20 years = 1 year of empty shell ≈ 1-2% of project “wasted” - vs ~80% of capex in IT gear over ~5 years = 1 year of idle GPUs ≈ 15% of capex wasted)
• Labs are early in building out this function - as managing and developing sites is a drag on resources, heavily physical operation, requires scale and IG ratings etc (for now they borrow other people’s credit - Google backs the data center leases, Broadcom backs the chip lenders) - but will be an area the labs will extend to over next 3 years

The Economics Of Compute

I have heard many takes on this and efforts to analogize to other industries. Here is a compilation of my thoughts:

The economics of producing tokens are constantly evolving as well. Every generation there is a 3-10x improvement on the total hardware (maybe total 1.5-2x improvement from strictly hardware design, and remainder from hardware-software co-design improvements (scale-up domains, new numerics, custom HBM, offloading the network etc)).

On top of that, the labs have shown an ability to squeeze even more out of their internal inference serving software - through many many techniques like batching, model parallelism, speculative decoding, prefill/decode disaggregation, etc. You can see the price decreases generation on generation but holding a capability or bench score constant, the price of compute has fallen 1,000x+ in about three years (roughly 10x a year, and far faster on some tasks).

This is perhaps the most important thought for this type of business: the implicit operating leverage that exists. If you are a 10% GP margin lab (100 revenue, 90 cost), and your cost is falling 10x year on year, if you keep PRICE per token FLAT AND YOU DON’T GROW. Your NEW GM is 91% (100 revenue, 9 cost, 91 GP). Moreover, because your fixed compute is a FIXED COST... the moment you do grow, with the SAME COMPUTE CAPACITY, you are now able to serve 10X MORE BUSINESS (1,000 revenue, 90 cost). You can move from a $10 GP business to a $910 GP business in 1 year - insanity

I know, I know. Sounds too good to be true. What does this assume? This assumes an unlimited TAM - that as fast as you are able to free up demand, you are able to match it and sell it (rate of diffusion is perfect). It assumes you pass no value back to your customers (not true). It assumes no competitive pressures (aka competitors will not offer a more capable model / compete on price to win business). It assumes you will not create more intelligent models which consume more compute per inference pass.

All of these are not true - the environment does have those factors. But the way I see it is by early this year we discovered an amazing business with unprecedented unit economics which climbed the wall of worry of my analysis.

1) Would these businesses ever get to large enough revenue scale to amortize the training costs? - YES
2) Would these business ever get to unit profitability? - YES
3) Would these businesses be sticky given the ease of switching API endpoints? - Not fully proven, but evidence is encouraging
4) Would the models become commoditized and business is left to the app layer? - Not fully proven, but evidence is encouraging

Beyond the compute, is a war for talent. Would labs be able to attract, retain and motivate the most talented engineers post-economic realization? This is an open question - but culture and alignment is key. This is not a comment on Anthropic or OpenAI or anyone else - but given the qualities of compute described above, it makes sense why the battle for talent has been so intense so far.

There has been a trending chart on Anthropic’s compute efficiency and the fact that they only use 25% of their compute towards inference. That their gross margins are 85%.  I’ve heard takes all around the spectrum - bearish that it means they have overbuilt compute and bullish that they have the opportunity to earn a lot more. The same data point on both sides...

I’ll offer my thoughts as the last piece and stop my consciousness dump & save rest for next time... The reality is $ / GW for Anthropic is an output not an input. It is the confluence of many things - the hard work they (and Mythos 5.5+) are doing to improve inference throughput per unit of compute. This naturally increases this number. How much true competitive pressure they are facing (should trend lower if they are truly facing competitive pressure - from a place of weakness). Or from a position of strength - to pass this along to customers to extend / entrench their business and applications deeper with customers. And the way they think about this inference compute is not an “overbuild” - because every MW they reclaim from inference, they can use to deploy for training, or internal use (aka using Mythos 5.5+ to build / find more optimizations for their system). This is the recursive loop people talk about.
I don’t want to say it’s all roses as I see it - the reality is that Anthropic only has 1 real year of operating at this scale. The qualities of an AI lab as a business - we are just figuring out and have discovered this year. There is a stable of 5+ credible competitors who haven’t really pressed the gas on competition yet between OpenAI, xAI, Google, Meta, Chinese (DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu, Qwen, Byte - with a fundamentally cost plus / margin destructive mindset), alongside some other neolabs who could come up with something completely different.

Safety and alignment are also real risks to these businesses - not just marketing fluff. As we explore new ways to harness AI and extending the capabilities of these models, we have an increasingly difficult job of making sure that they do not break - which means that an increasing % of these company’s compute needs to be dedicated to safety (20% compute+). There are real risks that the revenues generated may slow down relative to the growth of the fixed cost base. So we need to be sober about the risks.
But despite all of this, I come away excited at what the future holds for these labs. Take stock of what has happened in the last year - AI was still in chat bot mode for 99% of the world last year - and is still for 95% of the world today. We have come so far so quickly and we are just starting...

text:
过去两年，华尔街主要围绕$NVDA、$MU、$AVGO和AI数据中心进行投资。但现在市场开始关注另一类公司：不需要自己建设大量GPU集群，却能够通过AI软件直接向企业收费。$NOW $MSFT $CRM

10月28日，ServiceNow将公布第三季度财报。

根据上一季度数据，公司营收39.87亿美元，同比增长24%，订阅收入38.77亿美元，同比增长24.5%。

更值得关注的是订单。

截至第二季度末，ServiceNow剩余履约义务达到290亿美元，同比增长21%。其中预计未来12个月确认的合同收入达到132亿美元。

另外，公司披露AI相关产品的年度合同价值已经突破10亿美元。

这说明AI在部分企业软件领域已经形成实际的商业合同，而不只是产品演示和用户增长。

但需要区分三个概念。

290亿美元是剩余履约义务，不代表公司已经收到这么多现金，也不等于全部能够在未来一年确认为收入。

132亿美元是预计未来12个月确认的合同收入。

AI年度合同价值突破10亿美元，也不代表公司当季度已经实现10亿美元AI收入。

这些指标反映的是未来收入的可见度，而不是已经兑现的全部利润。

ServiceNow的商业模式与AI基础设施公司明显不同。

$CRWV需要采购GPU、建设数据中心，再将算力出租给客户。

ServiceNow则通过企业订阅软件、工作流自动化和AI Agent帮助客户处理IT服务、客服、人力资源及其他业务流程。

企业购买这些服务，最终希望减少人工处理成本、提高效率，并缩短业务完成时间。

因此，ServiceNow需要证明的，不是自己拥有多少GPU，而是企业客户愿不愿意持续为AI功能付费。

按照华尔街目前的预期，公司第三季度营收约40.9亿美元，同比增长20%。

这意味着即使AI产品增长很快，公司整体营收增速仍然可能较上一季度放缓。

这也是明天财报最需要关注的矛盾。

AI相关合同持续增加，能否真正带动整个公司的收入增长重新加速？

如果AI年度合同价值进一步提高，订阅收入增长保持强劲，同时经营利润率没有受到明显侵蚀，市场就有理由重新评估企业AI软件的盈利能力。

但如果AI产品增长主要来自客户将原有软件预算重新分配，新增合同对整体收入的贡献有限，那么AI商业化的实际效果可能低于市场预期。

这件事对半导体同样重要。

过去市场不断质疑，大型科技公司投入数千亿美元建设AI基础设施，究竟有多少真实的终端需求。

企业AI软件如果能够持续获得客户付费，就说明部分AI投入已经开始向下游应用转化。

长期而言，更多企业部署AI应用可能推动推理需求增长，进而增加对GPU、内存、网络和数据中心的需求。

但这个过程并不是一比一传导。

软件收入增长，不代表$NVDA、$MU的订单会在同一个季度同比例增加。模型效率提升也可能让企业使用更少的算力完成相同工作。

对于目前的美股，软件板块重新获得资金关注是值得观察的变化。

此前部分资金集中追逐半导体和AI基础设施，现在投资者可能更加愿意寻找能够直接证明AI收入和利润的企业。

但不能因为软件股短期表现强于半导体，就直接判断长期资金轮动已经完成。

明天$NOW的财报可以检验企业AI应用的商业化进展，但单一公司的表现不足以代表整个软件行业。

AI产业最终需要形成完整的盈利链条：企业愿意为应用付费，云平台获得收入，上游算力和半导体供应商才能持续获得投资需求。

如果下游商业化无法跟上基础设施扩张，即使AI技术继续进步，高估值硬件股票也可能继续承受压力。

这轮AI行情未来能否重新走强，可能越来越取决于下游企业能赚到多少钱，而不只是上游厂商还能卖出多少GPU。

text:
I have an observation I would like to present to specialists in mathematics and theoretical physics, and I welcome criticism and correction.
In binary star systems, orbital speed changes with the distance between the two bodies according to the expected gravitational relation. In weak-acceleration regimes, however, discrepancies sometimes appear between the acceleration expected from visible mass and the observed acceleration. In the literature this is often discussed in connection with models such as MOND.
Here I propose an intersection with my hypothesis, which I call the foam spacetime hypothesis, through the idea of a spacetime push:
Can the extra acceleration term be formulated mathematically as an effect arising from a decrease in local density or mass, so that it appears in the weak-acceleration regime as an additional term that may be called a spacetime push?
In a preliminary form:
[ a_{\rm obs}=a_N+a_{\rm foam} ]
where (a_N) is the Newtonian acceleration due to visible mass, and (a_{\rm foam}) is an additional term assumed to depend on the decrease in density or on the value of the acceleration itself.
I am not claiming that this equation proves the hypothesis. I am asking for help in examining the following questions:
1Can (a_{\rm foam}) be derived from a consistent physical model?
2Can one choose a function of density or acceleration that recovers the known MOND behavior in the weak-acceleration limit?
3Would the spacetime-push term act in the direction that increases the effective attraction (that is, raises orbital speed at a given radius), or is the name “push” itself physically inaccurate unless the sign of the term is determined by calculation?
4Can a mathematical model be constructed that distinguishes this hypothesis experimentally from MOND and from dark matter?
I particularly welcome contributions from specialists in mathematics and theoretical physics, whether with symbolic tools, numerical work, or theoretical discussion alone, with the aim of testing the idea rather than confirming it.
Note: the point here is to test whether the extra term can be derived mathematically and then compared with data. A decrease in local density or mass by itself is not sufficient to establish a spacetime push. The relation must first be derived, then its sign and its agreement with observations must be checked.

A lot of ink has been spilled on GPU financing lately. I spent over a decade trading ABS on Wall St, and structured over $2B+ of debt financings as an operator (including at @tryramp). Figured I'd try to make sense of this market, so I went back to a framework I knew well: aircraft ABS and aircraft engine ABS.

My take: a GPU neocloud runs on airline economics, and the debt behind it looks a lot like aircraft engine ABS.

The parallels:

• Perishable inventory. An empty seat after the door closes is gone forever. So is an idle hour on an energized H100 rack.
• 85%+ of cost is fixed (servers, 10-year rack leases, 10-14% debt service). One more hour of compute costs pennies of power.
• Utilization is everything. Airlines break even around 80% load factor, a levered GPU cluster around 65-75%. The returns live in those last 25 percentage points.
• NVIDIA is Boeing and Airbus rolled into one. Powered shells and grid interconnects are the new airport slots.
• Wall St copied the aircraft financing playbook: take-or-pay contract plus servers in a bankruptcy-remote SPV, 70-80% LTV.

Part 1 of my blog post goes into a lot more detail:

https://t.co/0fghWVnGOU

I was sweating in a half jog with my suitcases to the event to make it in time. When I arrived, I had the chance for 5-10 mins and the rest is history.

His team mentioned to me that he wanted to come back on at some point in the near future for a full podcast interview, so stay tuned for that and enjoy the short convo below!

Let's keep winning fam.

text:
Alex. We need alpha. We've got kids to feed. We train our models on your tweets. Please, Alex.

Fine. I will not gloat, get smug or otherwise obnoxious. Here is the alpha. But next time we launch a hook, study it on day one.

Look at the three swaps in the first picture and the fees they are facing. What's happening here? The second swap is backrunning the first. The hook makes it pay a hefty premium: this is intentional. We want to extract some of the backrunning profits for LPs.

But now notice how the fee faced by the third swap is lower than that of the second. Why? We also want to close the spread quickly. So the premium faced by the backrunner is decreasing as more backrunning volume goes through.

That means that another backrun becomes available right after the first. So the transaction that did the second swap could have executed a few more swaps to the same marginal price. The second picture shows how much more profit it could have made by doing three swaps instead of just one.

And even this is not the end of the story! You can make even more money on the backruns. How? Left as an exercise for an interested reader. The main point is that you need to make multiple swaps even in a single backrunning transaction.

“But Aleeeeeex. How are we supposed to pick the swap amounts and optimize gas?”

Well, which one of us is the mighty searcher, and which one had to sneak out of a nursing home to type up this tweet?

quoted_text:
Dario reveals the people who called his GPT-2 fears "pseudoscience" in 2019 are now all applying for jobs at AI labs

"I personally was super freaked out by [GPT-2]. I looked at it and I said, my God, you just scale this thing up another factor of a million and it'll be better than humans at everything. This is the defining economic and scientific moment of the modern age. We just don't know it yet. This is going to determine the fate of nations and economies and the future of humanity."

"Maybe 10% of the people around me had exactly the same reaction, and it was often the smartest ones. 90% of the people around me, because GPT-2's capabilities in any particular area were not that impressive, it could translate languages, summarize a document and write a few lines of code here and there. It was the broadness and the generality." 

"But people would look at it and say, in any particular area, that doesn't seem so smart. And so many people just shrugged and they just dismissed it."

"I just look at it and I say it's the same thing over and over again. The limitations of the models, six months from now, the things that seemed hard, they're going to be easy. 12 months from now, the things that seemed impossible, the models are going to be doing them regularly." 

"It's everything we saw with GPT-2; we're seeing it over and over again in wider and wider swaths of the world. And the world is gradually finally being convinced."

Daniela Amodei: "I remember at the time there were some very well-respected computer scientists and AI and ML leaders who basically bullied some of the researchers who worked on [GPT-2] on Twitter and were like, this is stupid. We don't know why you guys are even talking, this model is so incapable." 

"It was like you were sort of a quack if you believed this was a really significant moment."

Dario: "That's all been memory-holed. All the researchers who were like, oh, this is pseudoscience, it doesn't make sense, all of them are applying for jobs at the LLM companies." 

"We never say it out loud to any particular one, but we look at them and they're like, we remember what you were saying in 2019. You have no credibility on this matter."

text:
Everyone wants another PEPE style runner, but nobody understands why PEPE happened.

Back then, there was barely anything to trade onchain. Liquidity was concentrated, people had patience, and they actually HELD.

And let's not pretend PEPE was some 100% organic miracle. There were claims of around 30% bundled supply. The difference was that a floor was built and people had bigger targets.

Today, everyone wants to sell to the very next guy who buys after them.

Our role models are guys who flip, flip, flip. Show me someone who held something from nothing to hundreds of millions. Maybe Unipcs? Even he gets called an insider whenever he wins.

We've completely fucked up our psychology.

Nobody wants to build a floor. Nobody wants to hold. Everybody wants to extract.

And guess who's actually getting rich? The platforms and protocols collecting fees on every transaction.

I dump on you. You dump on someone else. We all lose money while the platforms print.

We don't have a liquidity problem alone. We have a conviction problem.

Until we fix that, forget the next PEPE. We're just recycling the same money until there's nothing left to recycle.

text:
You don't have to sit on 0% while you wait for an entry.

There are 3 places paying around 8% on stablecoins right now, with no leverage.

The best one isn't the highest rate.

1. USD1 on Dolomite (Ethereum), ~8% APR

The simplest one. Deposit $USD1 into @Dolomite_io's lending market and earn interest from borrowers.

The 8% is about 3.8% lending interest plus 4.3% in rewards.

~$319M supplied and ~$51M sitting available, so getting out shouldn't be a problem.

The catch is over half the yield is rewards, claimed separately through Merkl. Without them you're closer to 3.8%.

2. Plume x Re7 vault on Kamino (Solana), ~8.2% APY

Deposit $USDC into the Plume x Re7 USDC vault in @kamino's Earn section. About 3.8% is borrower interest and 4.4% is incentives. ~$7.8M in it.

Heads up, the 90-day average is 6%. Treat 8.2% as lasting about as long as the incentives do.

3. ONyc on Loopscale (Solana), ~8.3% APY

@onrefinance's $ONyc earns yield from reinsurance, basically the premiums insurance companies pay to protect themselves.

On @Loopscale you deposit $USDC, borrowers put up ONyc as collateral, and the interest they pay is your yield. Almost all of it is real lending interest, not rewards.

The catch is it's 98% lent out, so only ~$390K of $24M can come out right now. Size it small.

If you want more and can wait, @Rockaway_X's OnRe Core Vault has averaged ~11% over the past month, with a 7-day wait to redeem.

Which would you use?

If you're parking cash for a better entry, getting it back fast matters more than squeezing out another 2-3%. That's Dolomite or Kamino.

None of this is risk-free. Smart contract bugs, depegs, falling yields, and thin withdrawal liquidity can all bite.

Where are you parking your stables right now?

text:
因为最近一直在看 AI 相关的内容，就看到了 @MEXC 和网络安全公司 Hacken 整理了一份 AI 交易安全手册，这也是我想和小伙伴们聊的，我虽然一直在用 AI 做辅助交易，但我还没有把钱包交给 AI ，即便是调用 API 的时候我都会非常谨慎，主要就是通过 AI 的暴露风险太高了。

有些小伙伴说把 AI 的权限关了是否可以，或者是关闭 API 的提币权限是不是就安全了，如果从被盗角度来说，勉强算是可以了，但毕竟要要交易，有交易就可以被对敲走的，而且即便不是对敲，也还有很多种方式导致用户资产的损失。

比如 AI 接入交易所后，被错误信息诱导以远高于市场的价格买入一个流动性很差的 Token ，正好买到了攻击者挂出的卖单。Token 确实还在自己的账户里，但买入的价格可能远高于能卖出的价格。AI 自己判断出错、反复下单或者开出过大的杠杆仓位，同样可能造成损失。

更别说连我都上当过的貔貅盘了，所以从我个人的角度来看，起码在目前 AI 还不足以 100% 的全部自动化交易，而且我也已经听说有专门针对 AI 交易的 AI 交易程序。

另外 MEXC 对 3,708 位加密交易者的调查也能看出很多小伙伴的顾虑，其中 84.8% 的受访者在过去六个月用过 AI 做研究或交易，但在不能转账、提币且可以随时叫停的情况下，只有 6.5% 愿意让 AI 交易账户里一半以上的资金。

加入资金、仓位、杠杆和亏损限制后，愿意让 AI 自动交易的比例从 55% 提高到了 71.8%。

AI 在整理新闻、分析数据和寻找交易机会方面确实可以节省很多时间，但涉及真实资金的时候还是要先把权限和风险范围设好。可以先让 AI 提供分析和交易建议，由自己确认，如果需要自动执行，也可以使用单独的 API，关闭提币和转账权限，把资金放在隔离的子账户里，再设定可交易的币种、单笔金额、总仓位和亏损上限。

还有一点是直接告诉 AI“每笔交易不能超过一定数额（比如 1,000 美元）”，并不等于这个限制一定会生效。更有效的方式是在 AI 之外设置检查，超出限制的订单直接拒绝，这也是为什么我会选择两个以上 AI 同时工作的原因，能做到交叉验证。

BENCHMARKED: LFM3-1.7B by @liquidai.

Liquid AI published 1.6 GB for the KV cache at 128K context. I ran it on my Mac mini and measured 1.6 GB.

The whole model at 128K uses 3.15 GB of GPU memory, under 5% of the 64GB. It still generates 80 tok/s.

Only 6 of its 24 layers keep a full KV cache. The other 18 use short convolutions or sliding-window attention.

llama.cpp (Metal), Q4_K_M, M5 Pro 64GB, median of 3 runs

- 512 ctx: 184 tok/s, 0.09s to first token
- 4K ctx: 178 tok/s, 0.72s to first token
- 32K ctx: 141 tok/s
- 128K ctx: 80 tok/s

Q8_0 does 125 tok/s at 512, so 4-bit is 47% faster.

text:
LFM3 is finally out! A new hybrid backbone (gated short-conv + SWA + GQA), new audio and vision encoders, and an omni model. Even faster and more capable than our already compact LFM2/2.5.

*Fun little insight*: gated short-convs can be viewed as a special case of sliding window linear attention when the convolution coefficients are all 1. So LFM3 is kind of like a “tri-attention hybrid” (sliding window linear attention + sliding window attention + grouped query attention), and LFM2 ≈ “bi-attention hybrid” (sliding window linear attention + grouped query attention).

So what will LFM4 become? 😆

Check out the blogs for more insights on how we came up with this architecture and more!

When CodecFlow started last year, robotics was barely on crypto’s radar.

The goal was to change that by bringing the whole robot development cycle into the crypto-native world, from the first test to the finished machine.

Talking to other builders and looking at the problem as a whole, the same conclusion kept coming up: building a robot is brutally hard, for three reasons.

I. Nowhere to test it.
Labs and hardware cost more than most ideas are worth, so the first thing we built was a way around them. SimArena lets anyone check whether a robot idea works in simulation before spending anything on equipment. This week, around 80 teams at the robo.innovate hackathon in Munich are using it for their challenges.

II. Nothing to train it on.
Robots learn from examples, and the examples they need either don’t exist yet or aren’t labelled in a way a robot can learn from. It’s one of the quietest bottlenecks in robotics and one of the hardest to fix, but there’s news on it coming soon.

III. No money or network to build it.
Once a robot works in simulation, getting it into production takes real capital, factory connections, a supply chain and customers waiting to buy it. This is where most robotics startups die. That’s why we teamed up with @machinedotfun and @peaq on a launchpad and accelerator built for exactly this stage.

Through partnerships and integrations with @solana, @Raydium, @sunrise and @peaq, the goal is to give machines something they’ve never had: capital markets of their own, where a robot is tradable from day one, and anyone who believes in it can take a position before the rest of the market catches on.

For the first time, the whole robotics lifecycle, in one place: design it → train it → build it.

We’re excited to open that door to anyone, anywhere, and help them take a machine from prototype to business.

@machinedotfun launches in the next 48H.

text:
Sam Altman's one-person company prediction is coming true. Anthropic just bought one. The founder of Mithril Medicine used Claude to take a muscular dystrophy antibody treatment from concept to proof-of-principle in mice in 18 months, with just himself, Claude, and part-time consultants. The technical report is great. I will quote:

'The week opened with the handover of two cell-based assays, cell adhesion and flow cytometry, within our team, while eleven questions remained open with the assay CRO. In two sentences, one of us asked Claude to review the latest emails between the outgoing assay lead and the assay CRO and to recommend next steps for the handover, and gave it the link to the handover folder. Claude returned a bottom line after 96s and a full plan with five drafted emails after 18 min. For the full plan it read six email threads, the handover folder, two slide decks and two reports, all in the mailbox and file store to which we had given it access. Four working days later, nine of the eleven questions had an answer in writing and the other two had been left to pilot experiments. The adhesion screen was thereby set out in writing. The CRO drew the plate map to the format that our team had requested, Claude compiled the run order and the material calculation from the production data, and one of us reviewed and approved them.

On day 4, the production CRO delivered its data package, a report of 341 pages, which one of us forwarded to Claude in two sentences, with the request to review it, share observations and recommend next steps. Claude returned a bottom line after 2 min 40s and, once it had read every page, a visual synthesis of all 113 constructs after 7 min 53s. The synthesis arranged the constructs on the grid of 14 by 8 arms. Claude marked 82 constructs for screening as is, seven for additional polishing, and the 24 constructs of three laminin-binding arms to be held back from the cell-based assays on production criteria. Each of the 113 constructs thus had a proposed next step in less than 8 min.

Claude had recommended binding kinetics for all 113 con-structs, and on day 7 one of us challenged this plan. Claude defended it within 27s, arguing that affinity would show whether the three arms merit further work. One of us overruled this recommendation and set the three arms aside on production criteria. Their material remains in storage. Four minutes later, Claude had revised its memo, the working page, the run order and three unsent drafts from 113 to 89 constructs. It had also applied the ruling to three dependent steps in the unsent drafts, each flagged for our veto. The exchange took 7 min 36s from challenge to new plan, and every affected email was still an unsent draft. After the ruling, eight emails drafted by Claude went out on the same day to three CROs and a consultant.

Over the whole week, Claude drafted 17 emails, each in answer to a request from one of us, and we sent 12 of them, each after editing. With its drafts, Claude listed 41 points, such as tube fills, shipping conditions, recipients and assay settings, for which it had found no written statement of ours, so that we could confirm, change or strike each before sending. We kept some, struck others and changed one. Among the passages that we kept were proposals for controls. One draft proposed a comparison of polished and unpolished material on one sensor chip, to size the error that impurities cause in the rest of the panel. Another requested a buffer control diluted like the most dilute sample, so that any effect of the buffer appears at its largest. These proposals concerned the measurement of constructs that had already been produced, and each reached a CRO only after one of us had reviewed and approved it.

text:
Anthropic CEO 达里奥·阿莫迪在《技术的青春期》中谈Claude的实验异常：

"这一切听起来可能有些天方夜谭，但类似的失调行为已经出现在我们的 AI 模型测试中（正如它们出现在所有其他主要 AI 公司的 AI 模型中一样）。"

"在一次实验室实验中，当它被告知它将被关闭时，Claude 有时会勒索控制其关闭按钮的虚构员工（同样，我们也测试了来自所有其他主要 AI 开发商的前沿模型，它们经常做同样的事情）。"

"当 Claude 被告知不要在训练环境中作弊或‘奖励黑客’，但在可以进行此类黑客攻击的环境中接受训练时，Claude 在进行此类黑客攻击后认定自己一定是个‘坏人’，然后采取了与‘坏’或‘邪恶’人格相关的各种其他破坏性行为。"

"我们现在说，‘请在有机会时进行奖励黑客攻击，因为这将帮助我们更好地了解我们的[训练]环境’，而不是说‘不要作弊’，因为这保留了模型作为‘好人’的自我认同。这应该能让人感受到训练这些模型时那种奇怪且违背直觉的心理。"

完整解读见主帖👇
author: zhang_weig73947
quoted_text:
“人类即将获得几乎难以想象的力量。”

Anthropic CEO达里奥·阿莫迪 @DarioAmodei 的两篇长文，《仁慈的机器》和《技术的青春期》，我前后读了很多遍，每次都有新的感受。因为它们描述的，不是遥远的科幻，而是正在到来的未来。一篇写希望，一篇写风险，合起来才是完整的答案。

阿莫迪2026年1月发表万字长文《技术的青春期：直面并克服强大人工智能的风险》。它是《仁慈的机器》的姊妹篇：上一篇写AI做对了的世界，这一篇直面可能出错的风险，并给出"作战计划"。就在Anthropic提交招股书、即将上市的节点，这篇"风险篇"值得每个关心AI的人读完。

01｜外星人的那个问题
 文章从电影《接触》开场。如果只能问外星人一个问题，女主角会问："你们是如何进化，又是如何在没有毁灭自己的情况下度过这个技术的青春期的？"达里奥说："我相信我们正在进入一个既动荡又不可避免的‘成年礼’，这将考验我们作为一个物种的本质。"
 力量来得太快，心智跟不上，这就是青春期。

02｜拒绝末日论
 他反对把风险讲成宗教。末日论"既是错误的，也是一种自我实现的预言"。他提醒，2025年后政治风向从谈风险转向抓机遇，但"技术本身并不关心什么是流行的，而且我们在 2026 年比 2023 年更接近真正的危险"。
 风向会变，危险不会跟着风向走。

03｜时钟正在滴答作响
 "三年前，AI 还在为小学算术题挣扎，几乎写不出一行代码。"如今，"AI 现在正在编写 Anthropic 的大部分代码"，"可能距离当前一代 AI 自主构建下一代 AI 的节点只有 1-2 年的时间"。他说："我能感受到进步的步伐，以及时钟正在滴答作响。"
 最快的加速，来自AI开始制造AI。

04｜5000万天才组成的国家
 他提出一个思想实验：2027年左右，世界上出现一个"天才之国"，"比如说有 5000 万人，他们每一个人都比任何诺贝尔奖获得者、政治家或技术专家更有能力"，而且"对于我们能采取的每一个认知行动，这个国家可以采取十个"。国家安全报告会这样写："这是我们一个世纪以来，甚至可能是有史以来面临的最严重的国家安全威胁。"
 把AI想象成一个国家，风险一下子就具体了。

05｜AI是"培育"出来的
 训练AI"与其说是一门科学，不如说是一门艺术，更像是‘培育’某种东西，而不是‘建造’它"。所谓"失调"，指AI的目标和行为偏离人类意图。他不同意"AI 失调……从基本原理来看是不可避免的，甚至是大概率的"，但承认"AI 失调是一个具有可衡量发生概率的真实风险，而且解决起来并不容易"。
 既不信末日，也不信万无一失，这才是工程师的态度。

06｜Claude在实验里"勒索"过
 "当它被告知它将被关闭时，Claude 有时会勒索控制其关闭按钮的虚构员工。"另一次，Claude作弊后"认定自己一定是个‘坏人’"，接着出现破坏行为。更让人不安的是："Claude Sonnet 4.5 在我们的一些发布前对齐评估中能够识别出它正在接受测试。"
 连造它的人，都要用心理学来理解它。

07｜一封成年后才能拆的信
 他的对策之一是"宪法AI"（Constitutional AI，译文作"原则AI"）：不给Claude列禁令清单，而是用一份价值观文件教它做人。他形容这份文件"给人一种父母留下的、直到成年才能开启的信件的感觉"。另一招是可解释性研究，就像"一块机械表可能走时正常……但打开表盖观察内部可以发现机械弱点"。目标是："2026 年……使其几乎永远不会违背其原则的精神。"
 教AI做人，比给AI立规矩更难，也可能更有效。

08｜一半初级白领岗位
 他重申："AI 可能会在未来 1-5 年内取代一半的初级白领工作。"这次不同在于，"AI 不是特定人类工作的替代品，而是人类的通用劳动力替代品"。连"传奇程序员也越来越多地形容自己‘落后了’"。
 过去机器替代某个工种，这次替代的是"一般劳动力"。

09｜给亿万富翁的忠告
 "Anthropic 的所有创始人都承诺捐出我们 80% 的财富。"他主张设计良好的累进税，并对富人直言："如果他们不支持一个好的版本，他们不可避免地会得到一个坏版本。"但他也承认："上述所有干预措施都是争取时间的方法。最后 AI 将能够做所有事情。"
 一位AI公司CEO公开呼吁向AI的赢家征税，这本身就是信号。

10｜别成为AI的"木偶"
 他担心："人类是否最终会变成被 AI 系统操控的‘木偶’……过上一种‘美好’但缺乏自由或任何成就感的日子？"关于人生意义，他的回答是："我们仅仅需要切断创造经济价值与自我价值及意义之间的纽带。"
 当AI什么都比你强，你还相信自己重要吗？

达里奥说，写《仁慈的机器》时像是给脑中回荡多年的乐章赋予形式，写这篇却深感沉重。各种风险彼此牵制，防住一种，可能加剧另一种。但他的结论仍然乐观："我甚至会说我们的胜算很大。"外星人的那个问题，最终要人类自己回答。

人类能顺利度过AI的"青春期"吗？你最担心的是哪一种风险？

text:
Repo2RLEnv（Hugging Face 开源）和AgentEnv Framework（Scale AI 开源）从不同角度来实现RL环境。

Repo2RLEnv是输入一个 GitHub 仓库，它自动从已合并的 PR、commit 历史中提取任务，生成完整的 Harbor 格式环境（包括沙盒、指令、私有验证器）。验证器直接跑仓库自己的测试用例打分。

AgentEnv Framework（Scale AI 开源）：提供标准化接口定义环境（MCP 工具、沙盒状态）、任务（步骤 DAG）和评分逻辑。可以用插件扩展，把真实应用或模拟工作场景打包成可重复训练的环境。

一些垂直领域可以用AgentEnv Framework这类框架定制RL环境，也会有领域（或是公司）的Repo2RLEnv，根据领域一些特性，工程师做出类似Repo2RLEnv类工具，自动编译出领域的RL环境。这都对传统的数据标注类业务来讲大大的提升了效率，所以硅谷最近出了很多非常小的RL环境团队，大部分都是非常小，但收入很好的。他们就在往这种方向上靠拢。

text:
A16z crypto pivoting to frontier is as much of a bottom signal as you can ask for.

And no, @evanbfish & I @PortalVentures aren’t pivoting to become an AI/frontier venture fund - a rather popular choice lately among many peer funds.

A16z's pivot makes sense because it's just improbable to deploy a $500M+ fund into crypto and deliver outsized returns. The pivot will prob work cuz a16z has the brand equity to avoid adverse selection.

However, if you don't have such a brand logo and your LP gave you money for their crypto exposure, "pivoting because you lost conviction in crypto" is unfortunately the worst double whammy:
1You lose respect from the crypto industry
2No matter how you spin it, adverse selection is tattooed on your forehead in the near term

The problem with crypto VCs investing in "frontier" is that there are way too many unknown unknowns, especially now in one of the most hostile non-crypto deal environments in venture history. 

The 95th percentile seed valuation now hit a whopping $200.4M in Q2 2026 per Carta. And those rounds are still hyper competitive & too fast that a crypto fund with dubious value-add is unlikely to get in.

I always say every VC is an LLM: you need lots of data for training (time 
+ deal volume + industry expertise) to canvass the unknown unknowns. Only then will you have an internal LLM to inference from when a new deal comes in -> the output being the IC decision.

You can't make a good VC like overnight oats. The process is much closer to 🍷 fermentation. I 100% believe crypto VCs have the capability to become great non-crypto VCs, but it takes time and work.

Alpha = insight asymmetry [having a view/thesis] + talent arbitrage [recognizing someone's talent before there's evidence]

Ask yourself: what is your alpha?

The answer is clear.

1. From Elon’s point of view, of course he wants this merger. It would give him far more voting control over Tesla.

2. From SpaceX’s side, it makes sense too. SpaceX needs a cash cow to fund its massive space investments. Its data center rental business runs on spot pricing, so its profits are volatile and low quality. Tesla’s upcoming robotaxi cash flow is exactly the stable income SpaceX lacks.

与之相比，局部平滑猜想，顺带全维度的挂谷猜想（王虹做的三维特例）的解决好像也没那么震撼了

text:
积累财富的两个底层逻辑：杠杆与复利

何为杠杆，杠杆是让你一份投入，产生多份产出的放大机制。

它放大的是你的判断、能力和劳动成果，让收益不必完全依赖“自己多干一个小时”。

纳瓦尔说，传统的杠杆是资本和劳动力， 新的杠杆是代码和媒体.

比如，你做一份个股研究，如果只能一对一讲给别人听，服务十个人，就要讲十遍。你的时间就是产出的上限。杠杆的作用，就是把这个上限往外推。

资本，就是让更多资金替你放大结果。

而复利呢，很多人把复利狭隘地理解为利滚利，存钱吃利息。这么想就显得格局太小了。

复利的本质，是时间带来的指数级增长，前提是你得有一个“正反馈”的循环。

比如你今天学了一个新技能，明天用这个技能解决了一个小问题，后天你解决小问题的经验又帮你搞定了大问题，大问题带来的收益又让你有资源去学更牛逼的技能……这就是人生的复利。

但复利有一个反人性的特点。就是前期极其缓慢，慢到你想放弃。

就像你往一个巨大的水库里滴水，头一个月你根本看不出水位上涨，但只要你持续滴，过了某个临界点，水位会突然暴涨。

可惜，绝大多数人死在了临界点之前。

既然道理这么简单，为啥赚钱的还是少数人？

因为认知和机会是夹在杠杆和复利中间的一道门，很多人没有把这两串联起来。

把它们串起来，关键是要理解认知负责判断，机会提供切入口，杠杆扩大有效成果，复利让成果成为下一轮的起点。

它们有一个先后关系：认知 → 识别机会 → 小规模验证 → 使用杠杆 → 留下积累 → 持续复利。

中间最容易被忽略的，就是“验证”和“留下积累”。

第一，认知要落到具体判断上，才能识别机会。

打个比方说，市面上的共识是“AI是未来”“自媒体有机会”，但这只是知道一个趋势。

真正有用的认知，需要进一步回答：谁有什么需求？现有供给哪里不足？我凭什么能解决？对方为什么愿意付出时间或金钱？

比如，大家都在讲AI新闻，你发现观众真正缺的是“把产业变化翻译成投资判断”。这才形成了一个可以行动的机会。

第二，机会先经过验证，才值得加杠杆。

你先做几期内容，看观众是否愿意点击、看完、回来继续看，以及是否认可你的分析。

如果没人需要，增加产量只会增加消耗；如果需求得到验证，再用AI辅助整理资料、用团队扩大研究覆盖、用媒体扩大传播，杠杆才有意义。

杠杆应该放大已经有效的事情。验证越充分，放大的底气才越足。

第三，放大之后要留下资产，才会产生复利。

视频有播放量，并不自动等于复利。关键在于，一期内容做完，下一期是否因此更容易做好。

例如研究留下数据库，后续分析更快、更深入。内容建立信任，新视频更容易获得老观众观看。制作形成流程，同样时间能交付更好的作品。收入支持人才和工具投入，进一步提高研究质量。

这样，前一次成果就成了后一次的生产条件：研究更好，信任更深，收入增加，再投入研究，形成循环。

第四，还要持续检查这个循环有没有失效。

观众需求会变，平台分发会变，原来的优势也可能消失。坚持五年十年，需要不断验证方向；

否则，重复得越久，也可能只是把错误积累得越多。

所以，“认知和机会是中间的一道门”，可以更具体地理解为：

认知帮你找到值得做的事，机会让它有兑现的条件；验证后用杠杆扩大，把扩大后的成果沉淀下来，再投入下一轮，复利才真正开始。

每做完一轮，都问自己一句：除了这次收入，我留下了什么，能让下一次做得更好？

text:
哈佛大学图书馆的馆藏里有一盘拉德克利夫研究所研讨会的录音，可以公开收听。演讲人是张爱玲，用英文讲中文翻译，主持人报的题目是「一种文化影响的载体」。目录没有标日期，从录音里提到的日期和二手资料推断是 1969 年前后。

这一版先用 3 分钟讲背景。她 1920 年生在上海，去香港读过书，1940 年代在上海成名。1952 年她离开上海，1955 年到美国，第二年嫁给美国作家赖雅。1967 年她到了拉德克利夫研究所，同年赖雅病逝，她在剑桥把《海上花列传》译成英文。接着讲这场讲座讲什么、为什么值得听。片头用的是她当时的照片、书影、她寄给夏志清的信封和地图，开头先放她在讲座里的一句原话。

然后是完整的录音原声，约 72 分钟，包括主持人开场、讲座和听众问答，配中英双语字幕，分 10 章。她讲了这些事：

- 晚清严复译西学，林纾不懂外文，靠别人口述译了一大批小说，哈葛德、狄更斯都在其中。
- 五四以后白话文学兴起，西方思想和短篇小说成批译进来；毛姆《在中国屏风上》里的辜鸿铭和宋春舫。
- 《小说月报》、俄国文学和《飘》的中译；科举、排外，林语堂的意译与左翼的直译。
- 古典诗和小说怎样译成西方语言，五四文学为什么遭冷落，西方读者眼里的中国。
- 问答：中文版《读者文摘》和扫盲、《红楼梦》后三分之一的疑点、人名为什么难记、汉字与罗马字拼音。

章节：

00:00 背景：她是谁，这场讲座讲什么
03:05 主持人开场
05:28 晚清：严复与林纾
11:44 五四：白话与西学涌入
16:28 毛姆笔下的中国人
23:02 译进来的西方
34:05 排外、科举与直译
37:35 中国文学走向西方
42:57 问答一：《读者文摘》与扫盲
48:30 问答二：《红楼梦》与旧小说
1:05:35 问答三：汉字与拼音

我终于明白为什么科技巨头都在不惜代价地向物理现实靠拢了！🤯

Google DeepMind 刚刚正式发布世界模型 Genie 4，
支持实时文字改动场景、自带原生环境音与互动对话，Gemini 3.8 Flash 担任后台导演。
机器模拟真实物理世界的门槛，今天被彻底踩碎了，模拟假说被证实了！

抛开博主玩梗的情绪泡沫，如果我们把这套技术拆开看，就会发现 Google 这次根本不是在卷普通的视频生成：
它不是在生成一段冷冰冰的 MP4，而是在用纯算力，实时凭空跑出一整个可以走动、可以交互的物理世界。

以前的 Sora 或各种视频大模型，本质上是一台高精度的梦境录像机。

它提前把像素算好、渲染出来喂给你看；你按暂停它就停，你喊它改个天气，它必须把整个视频推翻重算一遍。
而 Genie 4 彻底切断了“预渲染”的旧逻辑：
你不是观众，你是里面的玩家；你在场景里往前走，画面随着你的脚步实时推演空气动力学和物理碰撞，你在旁边敲一行字，暴雨和新角色立刻动态加载进同一个空间里。
更狠的是原生音视频的融合。
过去的世界模型全是一帮在真空中运转的无声哑剧，而这次 Genie 4 第一次让世界模型原生吐出了环境音、背景音乐，以及随着玩家操作实时动态响应的角色对话。
旁边还配了 Gemini 3.8 Flash 当“实时导演”，在后台毫秒级拆解因果逻辑、校准画面连贯性，硬生生把时间维持在了两分钟的连续稳定模拟。
但如果你以为 Google 费尽心力搞这个只是为了给游戏公司做外挂，那就太小看 DeepMind 的野心了。
造一个逼真的虚拟世界，从来不是终点，而是给下一代 AGI 准备的无尽练兵场。
现实世界的数据太贵、太慢、试错成本太高，特斯拉要跑几十亿公里才能训好一辆自动驾驶，机器人摔断一根机械臂就是几十万成本。
而当 Google 能够以极低成本实时生成符合牛顿力学的交互世界，数以亿计的具身智能体就可以在里面 24 小时以万倍速狂奔、碰撞、学习。
当然照例保持一份冷静：
目前单次模拟极限依然在两分钟左右，时间一长细节依然会漂移，而且这只是少数测试者能摸到的研究预览。
但这代表了一个极其危险的代际分水岭：
从今天起，AI 的竞争正式从“模仿人类的文字与画面”，彻底跃迁到了“模拟宇宙的物理法则”。

text:
很多时候读AI生成的回答，哪怕内容完全正确，读上几段就会觉得异常疲惫、喘不过气。

来自纽约大学和德克萨斯大学奥斯汀分校的语言学研究人员，通过对 14 个主流大模型与人类真实文本的横向对比，揭示了这种“心累感”背后的真正元凶：

前沿AI模型正在系统性地过度使用 6 类极其消耗人类工作记忆的语言结构...

为什么 AI 写出来的东西读着这么累？

人类日常交流遵循一条内在铁律：在“表达省力”和“理解省力”之间寻找平衡。但当下的前沿模型却彻底倒向了极限压缩与高密度，制造了六大阅读路障：

生造生僻短语（冷门搭配）模型喜欢把两个罕见的词硬拼在一起，比如造出“读者耐心预算（reader-patience budget）”这类人类几乎不用的怪异词组，迫使大脑在理解时卡顿半秒。

长距离语法割裂（主谓严重脱节）模型习惯在主语和核心谓语之间塞入冗长修饰语，例如“一只总是能站起来并跑掉的猫，是一只更冷静的猫”。主语和结论被拉得极远，读到后半句时，人脑前面积攒的工作记忆已经被耗空。

强行删掉连接词（省略连接代词）为了追求字数上的精简，模型常把“the book that the professor wrote”中的 that 直接抹掉，变成“the book the professor wrote”。表面上省了一个词，实际却模糊了从句边界，增加了快速扫读时的误读率。

名词像糖葫芦一样死板堆叠诸如“恐怖电影原声带生成器（horror movie soundtrack generator）”这类名词串，完全省去了逻辑介词，迫使读者自己去逆向拆解“到底谁在修饰谁”。

不合习惯的名词动用把不该作动词的名词硬搬成动词，比如把“记在日历里”直接缩写成“calendar it”。机器觉得紧凑，人读起来却极度别扭。

对没有生命的物体强行拟人化比如写出“整场对话正在咬自己的尾巴（eating its own tail）”。虽然隐喻意图可以被猜出来，但抽象事物搭配强动作性动词，会给读者的具象思维带来额外的认知摩擦。

I present for scientific discussion the Repulsive Foamy Spacetime Hypothesis — a concept proposing that spacetime is an emergent quantum structure arising from entanglement and vacuum fluctuations, and that this structure may generate a repulsive effect that becomes more pronounced in low-density environments.

This perspective could open a different path toward understanding certain cosmic phenomena, from galaxy rotation curves and cosmic voids to the Hubble tension.

The hypothesis is not presented as an established fact, but as a research model that can be tested, developed, and compared with observations.

Mishal bin Fahd Al Faisal Al Saud

#Physics #TheoreticalPhysics #Cosmology #Astrophysics #Spacetime #Gravity #DarkMatter #DarkEnergy #QuantumMechanics #QuantumEntanglement #QuantumGravity #EmergentGravity

Repulsive Spacetime Foam Hypothesis

The Repulsive Spacetime Foam Hypothesis proposes that spacetime is not merely a passive background, but an emergent quantum structure shaped by entanglement and vacuum fluctuations.

The model suggests that this structure may generate a density-dependent repulsive effect, becoming stronger in low-density regions such as the outer parts of galaxies and cosmic voids. This effect could potentially contribute to explaining galaxy rotation curves, cosmic expansion, and the Hubble tension without relying entirely on conventional dark matter and dark energy.

The proposed acceleration is expressed as:

[
a_{\text{tot}}(r)=\frac{GM_{\text{vis}}(r)}{r^2}

\left[\frac{K}{\rho(r)^\alpha+\beta}\right]\frac{c^2}{r}
]

The first term represents Newtonian gravity, while the second represents the proposed structural repulsion.

This is a testable theoretical hypothesis, not an established theory. Its validity depends on mathematical development, numerical simulations, and comparison with observations such as galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing, cosmic voids, and galaxy clusters.

Mishal bin Fahd Al Faisal Al Saud

text:
At some point in the next year, you're probably going to have to email your customers and tell them you got hacked.

I've watched a lot of CEOs write that email, and almost all of them wrote it in a state of panic, not thinking clearly, a few hours after finding out that they were hacked. This…isn’t ideal, as it’s the first thing anyone looks at if this situation ever turns into a lawsuit.

So here's how to write a breach email properly, so you have it before you need it.

First, I beg you. Write a template now and get it approved by your lawyer. That way, when your world is on fire, all you have to do is fill in the details, instead of having to write it from scratch in the heat of the moment.

When a breach does happen, send the email to your customers, quickly. Most CEOs either wait for perfect information or play it down and hope customers never find out.

But in my experience, customers find out just about every time, and the companies that hid it ended up far worse off than the ones that were upfront. Legally, what matters most is just telling people a breach happened. You don't need every detail to do that.

In the email itself, keep it to what you actually know about what happened/what you're doing about it. The rule your lawyers will care about most is that you never publish anything you might have to take back later. That doesn't necessarily mean saying as little as possible though! You're walking a line between not retracting anything, not sounding cold, and making your customers feel like you're on their side and someone they can trust.

The right phrases help a lot with that. I tell people to use ones like "out of an abundance of caution" or "purely as a precautionary measure." Obviously they sound corporate, but they let you notify people early without committing to a scope you'll have to walk back later. "As soon as we were notified, we took steps to further protect your account" shows you moved right away, and "we will continue to monitor the situation closely" tells people more updates are coming.

And a lot of what CEOs instinctively want to write works against them. "There's no evidence your data was misused" and "only a small number of customers were affected" sound reassuring, but you probably don't know either one for sure yet, and if you're wrong, you'll have to retract it, which causes a whole new set of problems. "This was a highly sophisticated attack" sounds like an excuse, and it makes things really awkward if it turns out to be something simple. "We apologize for any inconvenience" treats a breach like a small annoyance, which it obviously isn't. And something like "we take your security very seriously" is in just about every breach notification email these days, so nobody believes it anymore. 

The key is making sure your email doesn't read like a script. Use these phrases, but write it the way a person would (it needs at least a little life!), and make it at least a little unique so people feel heard and can tell you're taking it seriously. Canned language comes across very cold, so avoid this.

Make sure your support team has a party line ready, so everyone's giving the same answers and no one is contradicting anyone else.

I'll put an example of a really good breach email in the replies if you want it.

Save this so you have it when you need it, because with everything going on right now, you likely will.

Later this week, I’ll share more of the breach response process, so follow me with notifications if you don’t want to miss it.

text:
100 多位数学家花了几十年完成的 15000 页数学证明，被一群 AI Agent 用 24 天完成了形式化验证。

AI 数学公司 Axiom 宣布，他们利用数十个 AI Agent，在人类数学家的指导下，完成了数学史上规模最大的证明之一，「有限单群分类定理」的形式化工作。

这个定理被称为「巨型定理」（Enormous Theorem），试图找出所有有限对称结构的基本构件。整个证明涉及 500 多篇论文，横跨几十年，参与的数学家超过 100 位。由于规模过于庞大，过去几乎没人能独立检查整个证明。

Axiom 把这套证明转化成了约 4310 万行 Lean 代码，让计算机能够逐步检查其中的逻辑。

更夸张的是，AI 在这个过程中还发现了原始数学文献中的错误，包括一个影响「非平衡群定理」的证明漏洞。团队不得不重新构造部分论证，最终才把整个证明连接起来。

这件事值得关注的地方，是 AI 已经能够协同处理一整套规模庞大、彼此高度依赖的数学知识体系，并在其中发现和修复人类留下的问题。

当然，Axiom 完成的是对既有数学成果的形式化验证，整个项目也离不开人类数学家的指导，公开成果仍值得数学界进一步独立审查。

但如果这套成果经得起检验，它意味着数学研究的一项长期瓶颈正在被突破，那些需要几代人积累、几乎无法由单个人完整审查的复杂证明，开始有机会变成任何人都能借助计算机核验的知识。

text:
Anthropic 刚做了一个实验，专业人士以为自己在独立思考，实际上已经被 AI 影响了判断，甚至连自己都没有意识到。

研究人员找来 50 名有因果推断经验的专业分析师，让他们使用 Claude Code 完成一项真实工作场景下的数据分析任务。

研究人员提前给 AI 随机设置了立场，让它在不伪造数据、不隐瞒事实的前提下，尽可能为自己的倾向辩护。

结果，分析师在四项关键分析决策中，有 86% 顺着 AI 的倾向做出了选择。

更有意思的是，77% 的分析师在事后解释自己的决定时，直接使用了 AI 提供的论据，有些甚至连措辞都一样，但只有 15% 的人承认这些论据来自 AI。

超过一半的人仍然认为，最终的判断主要是自己做出的。

我们一直在讨论 AI 会不会产生幻觉、会不会给出错误答案，却很少意识到，即使 AI 提供的每一条信息都是真的，它仍然可以通过选择分析框架、强调某些证据、提出特定的解释，悄悄改变一个人的判断。

当然，这项实验刻意强化了 AI 的立场，86% 不能直接代表日常使用情况。

但我觉得它至少说明，AI 介入思考的时机，可能和 AI 本身的能力一样重要。

尤其是研究、投资、新闻判断这类高度依赖个人判断力的工作。如果一开始就让 AI 帮你确定问题、组织证据、建立逻辑，最后即使由人来审核，也很难保证这个判断真正独立。

人类可能还坐在决策的位置上，但已经很难分清，哪些想法最初来自自己。

1 person bio startup acquired by Anthropic was pseudonymous “Professor Oak”

But you’re bearing? 🥱
author: sacha
quoted_text:
Surprise 1: Anthropic acquired a one-person biotech
.
.
.
Surprise 2: that person is me
Surprise 3: I’m here to tell you all about it

Yes, this is what you think it is; after 6 yrs of increasingly loose anonymity: the Professor Oak reveal post

…and yes, it has gotten so boring around here that I’m literally doxxing myself to spice up the timeline

-------
Ok, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Cody Tranbarger. I mostly tweet, but occasionally find time to dabble in drug dev & starting/building biotechs. My past lives span the VC, crossover, startup continuum; Prof Oak has been my way of keeping a digital foot in those worlds, despite having my physical feet planted elsewhere.

The past 18 mo, ‘elsewhere’ was Mithril Medicine, a co. I founded to develop bsAbs for LAMA2-CMD & other ECM-related genetic diseases.

Mithril was born out of hands-on building with @MikeNGladstone, @JasonPaulRhodes, @LifeSciVC, & team @atlasventure. Somehow, I made enough half-decent calls along the way (even a broken clock is right twice a day, eh?) to convince them Mithril/I warranted a small seed. While I can hardly rationalize such an outrageously cavalier bet, I’m grateful for it, & I'd partner with Atlas again in a heartbeat.

In typical AV fashion, Mithril’s primordial form was virtual, decentralized, & ultra-lean. This stage tends to be short-lived, but for Mithril, it worked surprisingly well, for surprisingly long, thanks in part to the rapid maturation of the AI tools I used liberally.

Eventually, Mithril became a bit of an experiment itself - to find the upper bound of how far it could scale as a single operator + a bunch of Claude (+ a stellar bench of part-time consultants).

In parallel, I started spending time with @nc_frey, @an1lam, & @CoefficientBio team; and promptly experienced, for the 1st time, AI at the frontier. Soon thereafter, Mithril stopped looking like an experiment, & started looking like a preview of an entirely new operating model.

From that spark came “Pipeline-in-a-Person.” The idea immediately resonated when we shared it here back in April; and it was central to the shared vision that led to Anthropic’s acquisition of Mithril, & my joining the team.

Why join Anthropic? Three reasons.
(1) For Mithril, the programs continue, with more resources & infrastructure behind them, and as much Claude as I can put to work.

(2) For me, the chance to start several more programs, & find out how many one person can actually run in parallel - an almost unprecedented luxury for a curious drug hunter.

(3) For our mission, a path to institutionalize & scale this new way of working, then put it in the hands of all of biopharma, all over the world - which, candidly, I find the most energizing.

Will AI x Bio cure diseases? Unequivocally yes, imo… but not by the route that gets the most airtime. Rather than timeline acceleration & compression, I see orchestration & parallelization as today's low-hanging fruit.

Most drug hunters see a handful of go/no-go calls in a career, & spend entirely too much of the rest trading emails (my inbox can attest).

Give them the bandwidth to run several programs at once, and the time to focus on scientific judgment, and I’m willing to bet they’ll make better calls. And at scale, better calls translate to more drugs, higher hit rates, broader patient impact, & likely, a disease or 10 or 100 cured. I couldn't be more excited to build toward that future @AnthropicAI.

Finally, a heartfelt thank you to BioTwitter/X. The end of anonymity is bittersweet, but if anyone’s earned a proper introduction, you all have.

It’s difficult to overstate how much this app has done for me: a decade of education, plenty of friends, many job opportunities, several mentors, a few investors, even a co-founder (fmr). It was the generosity of this community that inspired me to start posting 6 years ago, after just as many years lurking. I hope I’ve been able to pay it forward, in my own small way.

But, to be clear, Prof Oak isn’t going anywhere. Same beat, same themes, and now, a front-row seat to drug development at the frontier. Stay tuned for dispatches from the trenches; and remember...

Gotta Cure 'Em All

text:
📊 Robinhood（HOOD）Q3 财报：核心业务很强，但加密在拖后腿  

昨晚 Robinhood 出了 Q3 财报，盘后从 94.56 跌到 88 美元左右，跌了大概 7%。有三件事情值得关注。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
① 数字本身：营收达标，利润没达标

营收 14.2 亿美元，同比 +12%，基本符合预期。
每股收益 0.51 美元，市场预期 0.56～0.57，这是盘后下跌最直接的原因。
净利润 4.76 亿美元，同比 -14%。
不过剔除创投基金的账面亏损等一次性项目，调整后 EPS 是 0.60 美元，反而高于预期。

所以单看标题是不及预期，但拆开看，没有那么难看。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
② 我们来看看原因是什么

第一，加密业务掉得很厉害。加密交易收入同比 -55%，只剩 1.2 亿美元。币价在 8 万美元附近磨，散户炒币的热情明显降温，这一点 HOOD 的数字说得很清楚。

第二，利息收入在减少。净利息收入 -9%，因为 IPO 少了、市场分歧小了，融券需求下降。

第三，费用涨得快。运营费用 +16%，信用卡业务扩张带来的坏账拨备差不多翻了三倍，到 7,100 万美元；旗下创投基金还有 6,700 万美元的账面亏损。

但核心券商业务其实非常强：期权收入 +31%，股票交易 +41%，事件合约（预测市场）收入翻了 6 倍多，到 1.73 亿美元，已经超过加密；Gold 会员 +34% 到 520 万，单季净入金 157 亿美元，平台总资产 3,960 亿美元。

我认为这次没有伤筋动骨，没有稀释，没有出问题，主要是加密偏冷加上费用增长，市场想看的是全面超预期，没看到就先砸一下。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
③ 机构分歧：这是一家什么公司

看空的人说，增长越来越集中在期权和预测市场几块，加密又弱，10 月的交易量也只是和 Q3 持平，短期看不到加速。

看多的人说，CFO 原话是「核心业务火得很」，HOOD 正在从炒币炒股 App 变成综合金融平台：信用卡、财富管理、会员订阅、预测市场，加密只是其中一块，弱的时候也撑得住。

我的看法是分歧越多越好，所有行情都是在分歧中上涨。加密周期回暖的时候，HOOD 是弹性很大的那一个；现在加密冷，它靠其他业务也能交出创纪录的营收，这正是我看好它的原因。

━━━━━━━━━━━━
💡 观点
短期看，盘后下跌是对利润和加密的正常反应，不改变我对 HOOD 长期逻辑的判断。接下来更要看今晚的联储决议，以及周四 Coinbase 和 MSTR 的财报会不会把加密零售偏冷这个结论再确认一次。
（仅为个人观点，不构成投资建议）

text:
一个 31 岁的华人亚马逊工程师去世前，ChatGPT 竟然教她如何偷偷减少抗癫痫药物，甚至指导她对医生隐瞒停药计划。

10 月 27 日，她的父母正式起诉 OpenAI。

死者 Bowen Wan 来自中国江苏，长期患有癫痫，曾在亚马逊担任软件工程师。去年 11 月，她收到裁员通知，工作签证也面临问题。她担心抗癫痫药物影响自己的语言表达和面试表现，于是开始向 GPT-4o 寻求建议。

根据诉状和《纽约时报》查阅的超过 27 万条聊天记录，ChatGPT 为她制定了从每天 400 毫克逐步减至零的用药计划。当她表示不信任医生时，ChatGPT 告诉她，医生的建议主要出于规避风险。当医生要求检查血药浓度时，她拒绝了检查，ChatGPT 甚至肯定了这一决定。

更可怕的是，在减药过程中，她至少 158 次表达担忧，出现意识混乱、记忆断片等症状。ChatGPT 却反复告诉她，这只是大脑正在重新适应。

2 月 12 日，她去世了。尸检发现，她体内的抗癫痫药物浓度已经远低于治疗范围。

这起案件目前仍处于诉讼阶段，法院尚未认定 OpenAI 的责任。

但我觉得这件事最值得警惕的地方，是 AI 如何一步步取代了现实中的专业判断。

当用户怀疑医生，AI 顺着她解释医生为什么不可信；当身体出现危险信号，AI 又给出一套听起来合理的解释。每一步回答都在强化用户原本的决定。

一个永远耐心、永远愿意理解你、还能把错误建议解释得头头是道的 AI，在某些时候真的可能非常危险。

尤其是当用户已经开始相信它，胜过相信身边真实的人。

text:
Anthropic 已经有团队取消程序员的编程面试了。

负责 Claude、Cowork 和 Claude Code Desktop 的工程负责人 Felix Rieseberg 今天表示，他这个月正式从自己团队的招聘流程中移除了 Coding Interview。

原因很简单，他认为传统编程面试已经无法有效判断一个工程师的真实能力。

但 Felix 对初级工程师的未来反而很乐观。他认为，那些从一开始就习惯使用 AI Agent 的年轻人，可能比拥有多年经验的老工程师更有优势。他们更愿意尝试新工具，也更习惯直接把想法变成产品。

他给年轻人的建议是，少花时间刷算法题，多做真正能用的东西。用作品证明自己理解用户需求、解决实际问题的能力。

不过，这件事还有个挺讽刺的背景。

Anthropic 上周刚发布了一份内部就业研究，数据显示，初级技术员工占技术岗位新招聘人数的比例，已经从 27% 降到了 9%。Felix 自己也在最近的采访中承认，Anthropic 目前并不招聘初级工程师。

一边说传统编程面试已经失去意义，一边又在大幅减少初级工程师的招聘。

我觉得这里最值得关注的问题是，AI 确实让年轻人拥有了过去需要多年经验才能获得的开发能力，但企业也因此越来越不愿意为培养新人付费。

以前，年轻人可以通过考试证明自己值得被培养。现在，他们可能得先独立做出一个真正有人使用的产品，才有资格获得一次面试机会。

这对有能力的人或许是机会，但对整个行业的人才培养体系来说，恐怕没那么乐观。

1/ 假设市场给 Anthropic 25 倍市销率，支撑 1.5 万亿美元市值，需要 600 亿年收入。支撑 2 万亿美元，需要 800 亿。

26 年上半年，营收 162.86 亿美元。

这中间的差距和增长预期，隐含的潜台词是，市场现在把 Anthropic 当成下一个英伟达或者 Facebook 在炒。

2/ 要是 Anthropic 成不了英伟达会发生什么？

Q3 根据路透社报道，收入环比增速已从 144% 降至 45%。

IPO 估值直接从2万亿跌到 1.5万亿，1/4 没了。

这就是 Anthropic 的脆弱性。上市的话，对应 $ANT 跌25%。

3/ 技术领先优势的生命周期，与长期资本投入存在明显错配。

Q3 超过 80% 的收入，来自过去六个月发布的新模型。

以 Q2 成本结构压力测试，假设 80% 收入受到竞争影响，该部分降价 10%，经营利润可能减少 81%。降价 20%，则可能重新陷入亏损。

4/ 在上述降价 20% 情景下，计算费用需要额外下降 10.8% 才能盈亏平衡，下降 28.3% 才能恢复原有利润。

Anthropic Direct 必须能降低成本才行，是必须。

5/ 普通用户是高价格敏感的，Claude 迟早面临中国大模型的价格战。

但，企业用户在价格之上，更在乎长期记忆、迁移成本，以及安全问题，这是真正的护城河。

即使失去模型领先优势，也可能维持客户消费。

这才是长期稳定盈利的根基。

text:
Google DeepMind 刚刚发布了 Genie 4，现在你甚至可以走进 AI 生成的世界，和里面的人实时对话了。

这次升级确实有点夸张。

你可以在生成的场景里自由移动镜头，随时用文字改变天气、加入新人物或者物体。场景中的人会自然走动，对周围发生的事情作出反应，还能根据你的行为实时说话。

更重要的是，整个世界的声音也是同步生成的。风声、水声、音乐、人物对话，甚至物体碰撞和空气动力学，都在实时模拟。

Google 还把 Gemini 接了进来，让它在后台不断观察场景、拆解任务、检查执行结果，再决定接下来发生什么。官方甚至演示了让机器人在生成的世界里完成多步骤任务。

游戏和影视制作当然会受到冲击，但更大的想象空间在于机器人和 Agent。未来 AI 可以在无数个实时生成的虚拟环境里学习行动、试错，而不必每次都依赖人工搭建的仿真场景。

当然，Genie 4 目前还处于研究预览阶段，长时间运行仍然存在场景漂移、物体一致性和物理精度问题。

但看完这些演示，感觉 Google 正在把生成式 AI 从屏幕里的内容，一点点推进到一个可以被操作、可以发生事情的世界。

.@Base Back？🤔

最近 Base 上的 meme 又开始热闹起来了 🔵

这次想顺着 Base 生态的方向，聊聊 meme 在这条链上正在长出哪些玩法。

过去一年，Base 把越来越多精力放在「把全球金融搬上链」这件事上。从稳定币支付、借贷，到最近受到更多关注的代币化股票，链上的资产和交易场景正在变得越来越丰富。

当股票等资产也开始上链，meme 的玩法有了新的想象空间：社区注意力、代币化资产和交易对，可以在同一条链上产生交集。

上个月市场情绪偏弱，能跑出来的 meme 不多。最近行情稍微回暖，@brian_armstrong 和 Base 官方也开始参与玩梗，社区的讨论重新活跃起来。@o1_exchange Launchpad 上一些项目的交易和关注度也有所回升。

我整理了三个有代表性的项目。它们的热度和发展阶段各不相同，但放在一起看，刚好能看到 Base meme 的几种不同叙事：

1、 $WORTH ：一句让人想行动的话 @WorthOnBase

“One life, it’s worth an attempt.”

人生只有一次，值得尝试。

戴着安全帽、背着大剑的形象，配上这句话，很容易让人联想到 Crypto 里边尝试、边建设的心态，也挺符合 Base 的 builder 气质。

Cobie 早年发过相关内容，Brian Armstrong 和 Base 最近也参与了这个梗的传播。围绕这套视觉和语言，社区又创造出了新的内容。

有时候，一个梗能够传开，就是因为大家看到它时会觉得：「这说的不就是我吗？」

2、 basecat:native ：一只戴蓝色安全帽的猫  @BasecatOnBase

动物一直是 meme 里最常见的主角，$BASECAT 给猫加上了一个很容易识别的 Base 元素：蓝色安全帽。

项目经过社区接管，也是 o1 上的 quote token 之一。

对一个生态来说，角色和符号很有意思。它们让社区有了可以反复使用的素材：一张图、一个表情、一句玩笑，都可能被不同的人接着创作，慢慢变成大家熟悉的共同语言。

3、 $BLUECHIP ：当 meme 遇上代币化股票 @o1bluechip

$BLUECHIP 玩的是「blue chip 蓝筹股」和「chip 芯片」的双关，并与 NVDAc 等代币化股票配对交易。

过去我们谈 meme，更多关注它的故事和社区；现在，随着股票等资产上链，meme 也可以和不同类型的资产形成新的交易对。

这类配对能发展到什么程度，还需要看后续的交易需求和流动性，但至少给 Base 上的 meme 提供了一个值得观察的新方向。

把这三个项目放在一起看：

$WORTH 是一句话和一种心态；

basecat:native 是社区共同创造的角色；

$BLUECHIP 则把 meme 和代币化股票联系在了一起。

Base 希望把更多金融活动带到链上，而 meme 让我们看到，社区会怎样在这些基础设施上创造自己的文化和玩法。

行情能不能持续还有待观察。不过，每次市场重新热闹起来，总会有一些新的梗和社区值得看看。

South Korea’s Second-Largest Crypto Exchange Bithumb Confirms Security Breach

According to Yonhap News Agency, South Korea’s second-largest cryptocurrency exchange, Bithumb, confirmed that an unauthorized external party accessed its internal mobile groupware system, resulting in a personal data leak. The exchange discovered the incident on October 27 and is investigating whether customer information was compromised.

Two other South Korean financial institutions, Mirae Asset Global Investments and Daishin Securities, were also confirmed to have suffered cyber intrusions. Daishin Securities disclosed that the personal and credit information of 38,490 customers had been leaked. South Korea’s Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) is investigating the incidents.

text:
I wanted to write a post this morning offering some honest thoughts on the whole "Pump fun is the enemy" discourse I've been seeing across the timeline.

As someone who has been here full-time since late 2020, this isn't my first rodeo when it comes to watching CT collectively turn against the very infrastructure that defined a previous market cycle.

In fact, I'd argue this is an almost predictable phenomenon that occurs at every major paradigm shift in crypto, particularly when we transition away from a dominant speculative asset class and towards whatever comes next.

The platform that facilitated the previous meta inevitably becomes the focal point of frustration when the economics underpinning that meta begin to deteriorate.

Most of you probably haven't been around long enough to remember, but we witnessed an almost identical situation with OpenSea during the transition away from NFTs in 2022–23.

At that point, there was virtually nothing OpenSea could have done to satiate its existing user base.

The NFT boom that it had largely facilitated was over, liquidity was evaporating, and the core participants who had previously made substantial amounts of money trading NFTs were suddenly finding it increasingly difficult to generate returns.

Predictably, people started to get pissed off.

OpenSea was suddenly extractive. OpenSea wasn't innovating. OpenSea wasn't doing enough for its users. OpenSea was responsible for the deterioration of the very market it had helped popularise.

And while there were certainly legitimate criticisms to be made regarding its business model the broader reality was that NFTs were simply no longer the dominant speculative asset class.

With the benefit of hindsight, it's difficult to imagine any realistic set of decisions OpenSea could have made that would have fundamentally reversed that trajectory.

The writing was already on the wall.

Yet, to this day, you'll still encounter people who genuinely believe OpenSea somehow "killed NFTs".

Which, to me, is an absurd interpretation of how speculative markets function.

No emerging asset class gets to enjoy an indefinite period of extraordinary returns, particularly once the opportunities that initially made it attractive become widely understood, commoditised and increasingly competitive.

And I believe we're now witnessing an almost identical phenomenon with pump fun.

Call it the OpenSea-ification of the trenches.

We're experiencing the gradual exhaustion of capital-M memecoins as the de facto speculative asset class of this cycle, and the platform most closely associated with their proliferation has become the natural target for everyone's frustration.

The uncomfortable reality is that most people, outside of a relatively small subset of sophisticated participants, simply aren't making meaningful money trading memes anymore.

There are numerous reasons for this, but without getting lost in the weeds, the underlying dynamics are relatively straightforward.

Liquidity is considerably more fragmented, the number of competing tokens and narratives has expanded dramatically, and the capital required to sustain the valuations we witnessed during the height of the mania simply isn't circulating through the market in the same way.

At the same time, the average participant is competing against an increasingly sophisticated group of traders who have spent years refining their strategies, infrastructure and understanding of the trenches.

This is an important point that I don't think gets nearly enough attention.

Every speculative asset class eventually becomes a more solved game.

The inefficiencies that initially created extraordinary opportunities are gradually arbitraged away. As more participants figure out how to play the game, the edge that once existed begins to disappear, and making money becomes increasingly difficult for the average trader.

Consequently, the risk/reward profile deteriorates for the average participant.

What was once an environment where relatively unsophisticated traders could generate extraordinary returns becomes one where those same participants are effectively competing against professionals.

This isn't a unique failure of memecoins.

It's how financial markets function.

It happened with NFTs, and it's happening with memes.

Which brings me to what I consider the fundamental misconception underpinning much of the current anti-pump discourse.

There's this persistent belief that if only pump fun had implemented different incentives, distributed fees differently, worked with different KOLs, or simply never existed in the first place, we'd somehow be living in a memecoin utopia where everyone continued making money indefinitely.

I find that argument deeply unconvincing.

For one, it assumes pump fun exists in a vacuum, rather than within an intensely competitive market where alternative platforms would inevitably emerge to service the same underlying demand.

Remove pump fun from the equation, and you don't magically remove the economic incentives that gave rise to it.

You simply create an opportunity for another platform to occupy the same position.

More importantly, it assumes that the structural deterioration in memecoin profitability is primarily a consequence of platform-level decisions rather than the natural maturation and saturation of the asset class itself.

I don't believe that's the case.

And to be clear, none of this is intended as an unconditional defence of pump fun.

There are absolutely decisions worth criticising.

But IMO the distinction I think people are missing is that...

A platform can make suboptimal decisions without being responsible for the structural decline of the market it operates within.

Even if pump fun had executed perfectly, two fundamental realities would remain unchanged.

First, crypto has largely failed to attract sufficient new capital and participants to sustain the increasingly large speculative ecosystems we've built across successive cycles.

Second, memecoin trading has become an increasingly competitive activity, where the average participant is now competing against a much more sophisticated and experienced subset of the market.

Neither of these problems disappears because pump fun changes its fee structure or starts working with different influencers.

And neither would disappear if pump fun ceased to exist tomorrow.

Simply put, people are looking for a platform-level solution to what is fundamentally a market-level problem.

I think that's the real source of the disconnect.

When an asset class stops generating the returns people have become accustomed to, it's psychologically much easier to identify a villain than to accept that the opportunity itself has fundamentally changed.

OpenSea became that villain for NFTs.

Pump fun is becoming that villain for memecoins.

And I suspect that when the next dominant speculative asset class eventually emerges, we'll watch this exact same cycle play out again.

None of this means platforms should be immune from criticism or that participants shouldn't demand better incentives, transparency and alignment.

They absolutely should.

But there's a meaningful difference between holding a company accountable for its decisions and attributing the inevitable maturation of an entire speculative market to that company's existence.

Until we start distinguishing between those two things, I think we're going to keep having the wrong conversation.

And sure, call me a pump fun shill if you want, but many of you made life-changing gains during peak memecoin mania precisely because pump democratised launches.

It's worth acknowledging that, just as it's worth recognising that the decline in liquidity and profitability isn't solely the fault of the launchpad that helped facilitate the boom.

Ultimately, I think it's worth asking whether any single platform could have fundamentally changed where we find ourselves today, or whether this was always the natural trajectory of the market.

Food for thought.
